trajectory_summary: The call opens cold with an immediate price demand, deteriorates through the middle third into open accusations of evasion and runaround, then resolves once the rep accepts verbal bill read-back and the customer fully cooperates with a 12-month data dump. It closes with a booked appointment, so the shape is mixed: real energy leaked through avoidable friction, but the rep held her ground on scope and recovered to a locked booking.

observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day and time were agreed and the rep confirmed a reminder call plan and text follow-up, meeting the booked bar; no co-owner or spouse was mentioned anywhere in the call so that field is not applicable.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: Last month, the last bill I got was $700.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep acknowledged the number with surprise ('Woah. Okay.') and explained it via weather/rate increases, but never turned it into an explicit reason-to-act against the utility (e.g., naming the $700 as what solar replaces). The flip should have landed around 02:08-02:23 where she instead normalized the bill as weather-driven rather than framing it as the target the bill-swap eliminates.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asked what interested the customer in solar (verify.interest_in_solar); the call moves straight from intro into cost questions and bill-swap explanation. The customer never volunteers a motivational reason beyond the cost question itself, so there's nothing distinct to flip.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: objection_inversion / multi-angle resilience under repeated ballpark-cost pressure
primary_coaching_focus.quote: I feel like I'm getting a runaround for, you know, for another reason.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The same cost-ballpark objection recurred four times and escalated from impatience to an explicit accusation of evasion before the rep changed tactics. This is the single most consequential and most replayable pattern on the call — the fix (acknowledge frustration + name the trade explicitly, per rebuttals.price_estimate_before_design) is concrete and coachable in one session.

key_moments.quote: just first thing All I wanna know is what's the what's the, you know, general range of cost for something like that.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is exactly the trigger phrase set for price_estimate_before_design ('give me a ballpark'). The rep's actual response covers similar ground informally but never uses the canonical framing ('totally fair to ask... 30 seconds... real numbers not a random ballpark') that would have named the exchange explicitly and likely short-circuited the four-round argument that follows.

key_moments.quote: Alright. Well, I don't understand why you can't just give me a general idea of what what we're talking about rather than wasting a lot of time.
key_moments.stewart_read: Second touch of the same objection — customer restates it more sharply, calling the process 'wasting a lot of time.' Rep repeats process justification instead of pivoting to the canonical redirect_to_design language.

key_moments.quote: Alright. Well, why can't you just take an average of per month? I I don't know how you how you do it. I mean, you're just giving me a runaround right now.
key_moments.stewart_read: Third touch — customer now uses the word 'runaround,' a clear trust-erosion signal. Rep responds with more technical justification (on-peak/off-peak, sunlight measurement) rather than acknowledging the frustration or flipping the objection.

key_moments.quote: You're still not answering my question. Just evading everything I want to know about what what's the cost of installation?
key_moments.stewart_read: Fourth and final touch, now an explicit accusation of evasion. This is the call's lowest trust point and directly precedes the rep finally landing on the working verbal-readback path.
